newsitem.title: ITALY: An independent northern Italy -- would it prosper?.
newsitem.headline: An independent northern Italy -- would it prosper?.

text.p: If Umberto Bossi's dream of an independent northern Italian state of "Padania" ever came true, the world would face a formidable new economic competitor ready to take on all comers.

Unshackled from Italy's backward south, whose growth has been stunted by a deadly mixture of rampant political corruption and organised crime, Padania would take wing and quickly turn into the workshop of western Europe.

That is the bold vision painted by Bossi, the fiery leader of Italy's Northern league -- who plans to declare "independence for the north at the weekend, and by Giancarlo Pagliarini, his self-styled prime minister of Padania.

But experts say that Italy's northern powerhouse, even if it cut loose from the ailing south, would soon find itself grappling with the same problems that are sapping the competitive edge of other industrial economies in Europe.

With the lowest birth rate in Europe and an ageing population that is putting huge strains on a generous welfare system, northern Italy is sitting on a biological timebomb that could undermine the foundations of its prosperity.

"A secession would be a selfish choice by a present generation which does not want to spare much of a thought for the future," said Pia Saraceno, an economist at Milan's institute for social research.
Nobody doubts that the north is far richer than the "Mezzogiorno" as the poor south is known. What is more, the south is falling further and further behind.

A recent report on the economic state of the south by the Rome-based think tank Svimez paints a picture of unrelieved gloom. Taken at face value, the cold economic statistics suggest that Padania has nothing to lose but its chains by severing all ties with the Mezzogiorno.

Between 1992 and 1995 northern Italian exporters reaped fat profits from an export boom fuelled by a lira devaluation as the economy in the centre and the north expanded by 5.8 percent. The Mezzogiorno crawled along, growing by just 1.7 percent.
Incredibly, labour costs in the south have risen faster in recent years than in the north over the same period of time.

"As a result of the slower increase in productivity and of the faster increase in the cost of labour, unit labour costs, which four years earlier were two percentage points lower in the Mezzogiorno than in the north, were by 1995 nearly six points higher," said Svimez.
"This shows a loss of competitiveness that can only cast a very worrying shadow on the prospects of the southern economy," the report added.
The Northern League's Pagliarini has proposed that a future state of Padania would have to be be complete with its own currency and central bank.

An independent "lira padana" -- as the would-be northern currency has been dubbed -- might have unfortunate consequences for thriving exporters if, as economists predict, it appreciated strongly against the German mark and the U.S. dollar.
"The northeast of the country has grown a lot as a result of the lira's devaluation," said Saraceno. "But if the lira were to strengthen they could find themselves in trouble."

The biggest bone of contention between north and south, if the two were ever to part company, would be agreeing on a share-out of Italy's enormous public debt mountain, estimated at 2,000 trillion lire.
The League's Pagliarini says the debt would be apportioned between the south and the north on a per capita basis, simply by dividing the total by the country's 60 million inhabitants.
Some economists have cried foul. They point out that more than two-thirds of the national debt is funded by northern households who profit handsomely from the interest payments on treasury bills.
In 1991, northern families grossed 56 trillion lire in interest payments on the debt while only eight trillion lire went to cash-starved southern households. $=1,510 lire
